distractors: Nine justices, appointed by the governor for life
Five justices, appointed by the General Assembly
Twelve justices, elected statewide at large
questions.explanation: Kentucky's highest court has seven justices, each elected from a Supreme Court district - unlike the nine appointed federal justices with life tenure. Kentucky elects its judges at every level of the Court of Justice, a deliberate accountability choice the federal system rejects.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Seven elected justices in Kentucky; nine appointed-for-life in Washington.

questions.question: A felony trial and a major civil lawsuit over a land dispute both begin in the same Kentucky court. Which court is it, and what kind of jurisdiction does it hold?
questions.correctAnswer: The Circuit Court - Kentucky's court of general jurisdiction, which hears felony cases and larger civil matters, and also takes appeals from District Court
distractors: The District Court - Kentucky's court of general jurisdiction for all trials
The Court of Appeals - Kentucky's trial court for serious cases
The fiscal court - the county body that tries felony cases
questions.explanation: Circuit Courts are Kentucky's general-jurisdiction trial courts: felonies, capital cases, and civil claims above the District Court's limit start there, and District Court cases appeal into them. Naming the general-jurisdiction court correctly is the key discrimination this question tests.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Serious trials start in Circuit Court - 'general jurisdiction' is the phrase to keep.

questions.question: A Kentuckian receives a traffic citation and faces a misdemeanor shoplifting charge, while her neighbor files a small-claims case. In Kentucky, all three matters are handled by:
questions.correctAnswer: The District Court - the court of limited jurisdiction for traffic cases, misdemeanors, small claims, and preliminary hearings in felony cases
distractors: The Circuit Court, which tries every case filed in Kentucky
The Court of Appeals, sitting as a trial court for minor matters
City police courts operating outside the Court of Justice
questions.explanation: District Courts handle the high-volume end of Kentucky justice: traffic, misdemeanors, small claims, juvenile matters, and felony preliminary hearings. 'Limited jurisdiction' is not a judgment of importance - it is the defined list of case types the constitution and statutes assign to that level.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Traffic, misdemeanors, small claims - District Court is Kentucky's front door of justice.

questions.question: County business in Kentucky - roads, budgets, ordinances - is conducted by a body whose name surprises students from other states. It is the:
questions.correctAnswer: Fiscal court - the county's legislative and administrative body, made up of the county judge/executive and the magistrates (or commissioners)
distractors: County supreme court, which also tries the county's felony cases
Board of aldermen, appointed by the governor for each county
County council of mayors from every city in the county
questions.explanation: Despite its name, the fiscal court is not a court of law at all - it is county government in legislative form, a relic of older terminology kept by the Kentucky Constitution. Judicial work belongs to the Court of Justice; the fiscal court handles money, roads, and county services.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The fiscal court spends and legislates - despite the name, it judges nothing.

questions.question: KRS 158.141(5) requires students to learn the roles of state and local governments. In a Kentucky county, the county judge/executive's role is best described as:
questions.correctAnswer: The county's chief executive - presiding over the fiscal court and administering county government; the judging in the office's old title moved to the real courts with the 1975 Judicial Article
distractors: The county's chief trial judge, presiding over felony trials
An honorary title with no executive responsibilities
The official who appoints the county's state legislators
questions.explanation: The title is a fossil: before the 1975 Judicial Article, county judges did judge. Today the county judge/executive is the county's elected chief executive - fiscal court presiding officer and administrator - while real judging moved to District and Circuit Courts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Judge in the name, executive in the job - the 1975 reforms moved the judging out.

questions.question: Kentucky is divided into how many counties - a number often used to explain why Kentucky has so much local government?
questions.correctAnswer: 120 counties
distractors: 100 counties
88 counties
254 counties
questions.explanation: Kentucky's 120 counties give it the third-most counties of any state (behind Texas and Georgia) and one of the densest maps of local government in the country - a concrete anchor for KRS 158.141(5)'s state-and-local-roles requirement.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 120 counties - Kentucky packs a lot of local government into one state.

questions.question: A Kentucky city council passes an ordinance setting rules for sidewalk cafes, while the General Assembly sets the statewide speed limits and criminal code. The pairing illustrates which principle from KRS 158.141(5)?
questions.correctAnswer: State government and local governments have different roles: cities handle local services and ordinances under state law, while the state sets the general law for the whole Commonwealth
distractors: Local governments are sovereign and may override state law within city limits
Cities may set criminal codes but not traffic rules
The state government may not legislate on anything a city has regulated first
questions.explanation: Kentucky cities draw their authority from the state constitution and statutes (including home-rule powers), and they govern daily-life matters - streets, utilities, zoning, local services. The General Assembly writes the laws of general application. Neither level is sovereign over the other the way the states and the federal government divide sovereignty in federalism.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ordinances for daily life locally; general law from the state - roles, not rivals.

questions.question: Which scenario best shows the correct division of roles among Kentucky's levels of government?
questions.correctAnswer: The county fiscal court funds and maintains county roads, the city operates its water utility, the state maintains the interstate highways, and the federal government sets the standards the state's elections office implements for federal elections
distractors: The city council sets the statewide income tax, and the fiscal court declares Kentucky's foreign policy
The General Assembly hires the county's road crew, and the governor appoints every city council
The fiscal court issues U.S. passports, and the city council coins money for local use
questions.explanation: Each level does the work assigned to it: counties run county infrastructure, cities run municipal services, the state runs state highways and general law, and the federal government handles national functions. Coining money and foreign policy are federal-only; appointing local officials from Frankfort would erase the local role KRS 158.141(5)(e) requires students to learn.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Match the job to the level - roads, water, highways, and passports each have a correct home.

questions.question: HS.C.KGO.3 asks how active citizens can affect change in their Kentucky communities. Which action is a direct example at the local level?
questions.correctAnswer: Attending a fiscal court meeting and speaking during public comment about a county road problem
distractors: Refusing to pay county property taxes until the road is fixed
Writing to the president to report the county road
Waiting for the next census to redraw the county
questions.explanation: KGO.3's point is that Kentucky government is reachable: fiscal courts, city councils, and school boards all meet publicly and hear residents, and a citizen who shows up and speaks is participating in governing, not merely observing it. Tax refusal is lawbreaking, not participation, and the road is a county responsibility the president has no power over.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Show up and speak where the decision sits - that is KGO.3 in action.

questions.question: A Frankfort bill would change a law a Kentucky student cares about. The most direct way for her to act on it as a citizen this week is to:
questions.correctAnswer: Contact her own state representative and state senator - by call, email, or a visit - and state her position before the vote
distractors: Call the White House and ask the president to veto the state bill
Ask the Kentucky Supreme Court to block the bill before passage
File a federal lawsuit against the General Assembly
questions.explanation: Kentucky legislators represent small enough districts that constituent contact genuinely registers, and the General Assembly publishes member contacts and bill status for exactly this purpose. Presidents do not veto state bills, and courts review laws after enactment, not before - the citizen's timely tool is her own two legislators.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Your representative and your senator, before the vote - constituent contact is the lever.

questions.question: Beginning with the class entering grade 9 in 2025-26, Kentucky's civic-literacy graduation requirement (KRS 158.141) gives each local board a choice. What is the choice?
questions.correctAnswer: Either require a half-credit civic-literacy course with the content the statute lists, or require students to pass the 100-question civics test drawn from the U.S. naturalization test
distractors: Either require a full year of Kentucky history, or waive civics entirely
Either require the state civics test at a 60 percent passing score, or require community service instead
Either test students on the U.S. Constitution only, or on the Kentucky Constitution only
questions.explanation: HB 535 (2024) rewrote KRS 158.141: districts choose the half-credit course - whose statutory content includes both constitutions and the roles of state and local government - or the USCIS-drawn test. The old form of the law (a test for everyone) no longer describes the requirement.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Course or test - the district chooses, but every student takes one of the two paths.

questions.question: A Kentucky district chooses the test path under KRS 158.141 as amended by HB 535 (2024). Which pair of numbers is now correct for that test?
questions.correctAnswer: 100 questions drawn from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services naturalization test, with a passing score of 70 percent
distractors: 100 questions drawn from Kentucky's own state test bank, with a passing score of 60 percent
128 questions drawn from the U.S. naturalization test, with a passing score of 70 percent
60 questions drawn from the naturalization test, with a passing score of 60 percent
questions.explanation: HB 535 kept the 100-question USCIS source but raised the passing score from 60 to 70 percent for the entering class of 2025-26 onward, while adding the course alternative. Older summaries still circulating with the 60 percent figure describe the superseded law - the exact trap this question tests.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 100 questions, 70 to pass - the 60 percent figure is the old law.

questions.question: Compared with the U.S. Constitution, Kentucky's 1891 constitution is best described as:
questions.correctAnswer: Much longer and more detailed, covering many specific policies, and far more frequently amended - because state constitutions handle the whole range of everyday governing that the federal frame leaves to statutes
distractors: Shorter and more general, and almost never amended since 1891
Identical in length, because state constitutions must mirror the federal text
Longer, but impossible to amend under any circumstances
questions.explanation: The U.S. Constitution is a short frame of government amended 27 times in over 230 years. Kentucky's 1891 document runs to tens of thousands of words, legislates in constitutional text on subjects like taxation and local government, and has been amended dozens of times - the typical state pattern, and KGO.2's central comparative insight.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: States write constitutions like detailed rulebooks; the federal one is a frame - length and amendment counts prove it.
